about: Statements typed by hand from sources with no machine-readable form: NASA's Orbital Debris Quarterly News after the 16th edition's cut-off, the U.S. Space Forces-Space notice on Space-Track's login page, named analysts and news reports (2024 to 2026), and the catalogue itself where fragments were published with no report. ESA's Space Environment Report tables are typed apart, in data/truth/esa-ser.json, and the quarterly news issues read are listed in data/truth/odqn-coverage.json. Each statement cites where it was read, and each was read by a person: typed here, or given to npm run truth:add, by hand or through the breakup-report form the owner accepts, which checks it and appends it in this layout. Never derived by a program.

statements.ref: ODQN 26(3), September 2022, p. 2
statements.causeStated: unknown; a collision with an unknown, small or untracked object is called a logical explanation
statements.note: Identified by the 18th Space Defense Squadron. 52 pieces by late July 2022.

statements.ref: ODQN 27(1), March 2023, pp. 1-2; ODQN 28(4), October 2024, p. 2
statements.causeStated: accidental explosion (the ODQN's top-ten table); passivation or insulation suspected

statements.ref: U.S. Strategic Command, whose Joint Space Operations Center then ran the space surveillance network: Brig. Gen. Michael Carey's statement as reported by Spaceflight Now on 2009-02-11 (https://spaceflightnow.com/news/n0902/11iridium/)

event.stated: Tuesday, 10 February 2009 (the article's dating of the collision)

statements.causeStated: the collision of Iridium 33 and Cosmos 2251 (the article)
statements.note: "As of about 12 hours ago, I think the head count was up (to around) 600 pieces." "It's going to take about two days before we get a solid picture of what the debris fields look like." The count is of both satellites' pieces. The command held the role the U.S. Space Forces hold now.

statedOn.ref: Spaceflight Now, 11 February 2009: the command's spokesman spoke on the article's day
